la:verb:admitto.html:
ad-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a. (admĭsse
sync. for admisisse, : admittier arch. for admitti, as ), orig. to send to; hence with the access. idea of leave, permission (cf.: aditus, accessus), to suffer to come or go to a place, to admit.—Constr. with in and acc. (in and abl. is rare and doubtful), ad, or dat. (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: ad eam non admissa sum,; so Eun. 2, 2, 50: quam multis custodibus opus erit, si te semel ad meas capsas admisero,: in cubiculum,: lucem in thalamos,: domum ad se filium,: plebem ad campestres exercitationes,: aliquem per fenestram,; cf. : admissis intra moenia hostibus,.—
Esp.
Of those who admitted one on account of some business; and under the emperors, for the purpose of salutation, to allow one admittance or access, to grant an audience (the t. t. for this; v. admissio, admissionalis; opp. excludere,; ; cf. Schwarz ad h. 1. 47, 3): nec quemquam admisit,admitted no one to his presence,: domus clari hominis, in quam admittenda hominum cujusque modi multitudo,: Casino salutatum veniebant; admissus est nemo,; ; ; : spectatum admissi,: admittier orant,: turpius eicitur quam non admittitur hospes,: vetuit ad eum quemquam admitti,; : promiscuis salutationibus admittebat et plebem,.—Metaph.: ante fores stantem dubitas admittere Famam,.—
Of a harlot: ne quemquam interea alium admittat prorsus quam me ad se virum,; .—Also of the breeding of animals, to put the male to the female (cf.: admissarius, admissura, admissus),; ; ; cf. ; ; ; .—Also used of the female of animals, , and .—
Admittere aliquem ad consilium, to admit one to counsel or consultation: nec ad consilium casus admittitur,: horum in numerum nemo admittebatur nisi qui, etc., Halm.—Hence: admittere aliquem ad honores, ad officium,to admit him to, to confer on,; ; ; .—
Of a horse, to let go or run, to give loose reins to (cf.: remittere, immittere, less emphatic than concitare; usu. in the part. perf.): admisso equo in mediam aciem irruere,: equites admissis equis ad suos refugerunt,: Considius equo admisso ad eum accurrit,came at full speed,: in Postumium equum infestus admisit,; so ; .—Hence of the hair, to let it flow loosely: admissae jubae,

Fig.
Of words, entreaties, etc., to permit a thing to come, to give access or grant admittance, to receive: pacis mentionem admittere auribus,; so 30, 3: nihil quod salutare esset, ad aurĭs admittebant,: quo facilius aures judicum, quae post dicturi erimus, admittant,.—Hence also absol.: admittere precationem,to hear, to grant, Gron.; : tunc admitte jocos, give admittance to jesting, i. e. allow it, .—So also: aliquid ad animum,: cogitationem,.—
Of an act, event, etc., to let it be done, to allow, permit (fieri pati, Don. ad ).—With acc. of thing: sed tu quod cavere possis stultum admittere est, Ter. l. c.: quod semel admissum coërceri non potest,: non admittere litem,: aspicere ecquid jam mare admitteret,: non admittere illicita,.—With subj. clause: hosti non admissuro, quo minus aggrederetur,.—With acc. and inf.: non admisit quemquam se sequi,; so acc. of person alone: non admisit eum,.—Hence, in the language of soothsayers, t. t. of birds which give a favorable omen, = addīco, to be propitious, to favor: inpetritum, inauguratum'st, quovis admittunt aves,: ubi aves non admisissent,; (hence: ADMISSIVAE: aves, in Paul. ex . Müll.).—
Of an unlawful act, design, etc., to grant admittance to one's self; hence, become guiliy of, to perpetrate, to commit (it thus expresses rather the moral liability incurred freely; while committere designates the overt act, punishable by civil law, Herz. ad ; freq. and class.), often with a reflexive pron., in me, etc. (acc.): me hoc delictum admisisse in me, vehementer dolet,: ea in te admisisti quae, etc.,: tu nihil admittes in te formidine poenae,: admittere in se culpam,; : scelera, quae in se admiserit, Müll.: quid umquam Habitus in se admisit, ut, etc.,: quantum in se facinus,.—And without such reflexive pron.: cum multos multa admĭsse acceperim,: quid ego tantum sceleris admisi miser?; so, si Milo admisisset aliquid, quod, etc.,: dedecus,: commissum facinus et admissum dedecus confitebor,: tantum dedecus,: si quod facinus,: flagitium,: fraudem,: maleficium,: scelus,: facinus miserabile,: pessimum facinus pejore exemplo,: tantum dedccoris,; so 2, 37; 3, 59 al.

la:verb:admoneo.gloss: to remind, recall to the mind, make remember
senses: to remind, recall to the mind, make remember
la:verb:admoneo.html:
ad-mŏnĕo, ui, ĭtum, 2, v. a.,
to bring up to one's mind, to put one in mind of (in a friendly manner), to remind, suggest, advise, warn, admonish (by influencing more directly the reason and judgment; while in adhortor the admonition is addressed immediately to the will, Doed. Syn. 1, 164: Moneo, et admoneo hoc differunt, quod monemus futura, admonemus praeterita; illa ut caveamus et discamus, haec ut recordemur, ; cf. Ellendt ad : in monente benevolentia, in admonente memoria, Ernest. no. 1663).
In gen., constr. absol. and with aliquem alicujus rei or de aliqua re, aliquam rem (Sallust employs them all); with ut or ne. when an action follows; with acc. and inf. or a rel. clause, when merely an historical

fact is brought to view, Zumpt, § 439 and 615.

Absol.: qui admonent amice, docendi sunt,: amicissime admonere,: si sitis admoneret, profluente aquā vitam tolerat,: admonitus in somnis,.—
Aliquem alicujus rei: admonebat alium egestatis, alium cupiditatis suae,: quoniam nos tanti viri res admonuit,: admonere aliquem foederis,; : judices legum et religionis,: admonitus hujus aeris alieni,: aetatis et condicionis admoneri,; cf. Drak. ad .—And with acc. of person omitted: adversae res admonuerunt religionum,; : veterum recentiumque admonens,.—
Aliquem de aliqua re: de aede Telluris et de porticu Catuli me admones,: ut aliquid aliquando de doctrinae studiis admoneamur,: de moribus civitatis tempus admonuit,: admonuit eos de auxiliis Dei,.—Sometimes in passing from a subject already discussed to a new one, = docere, dicere, to treat of, to speak of: de multitudine (verborum) quoniam quod satis esset admonui, de obscuritate pauca dicam, Müll.—
With two acc. (in gen., only with illud, istuc, quod, multa, res, etc.): ridiculum est te istuc me admonere,: illud te esse admonitum volo,: jam illud non sunt admonendi, ut, etc.,: illud me praeclare admones,: sin quippiam essem admonitus,: multa praeterea ostentis, multa extis admonemur,: eam rem nos locus admonuit,.— (ε) With acc. and inf.: admonuisti etiam dictum aliquod in petitionem tuam dici potuisse, B. and K.: et meminerant et admonebant alii alios, supplicium ex se, non victoriam peti,: nostri detrimento admonentur diligentius stationes disponere, Auct. B. G. 8, 12.—(ζ) With a rel. clause: meus me sensus, quanta vis fraterni sit amoris, admonet,.—(η) With ut or ne: admonebat me res, ut, etc.,: Caninius noster me tuis verbis admonuit, ut scriberem,: ea res admonet, ut, etc.,; so, corresp. with moneo,.—(θ) With the simple subj. (in the historians): simulque admonerent liberis suis prospiceret,: nisi Seneca admonuisset venienti matri occurreret,: admonuit negotiis abstineret,: illud me admones, cum illum videro, ne nimis indulgenter, et cum gravitate potius loquar, (where ut is to be supplied from the preceding ne).—(ι) With a simple inf. (so most freq. after the Aug. per., but also in Cic.): ut mos erat istius atque ut eum suae libidines facere admonebant,: easdem decedere campis admonuit,; so, Matrem Admonuit ratibus sacris depellere taedas,: sol acrior ire lavatum admonuit,; so ; : nihil agere quod non prosit, fabella admonet,; : regrediendum (sc. esse sibi),.—(κ) With ad and the gerund.: ad thesaurum reperiendum,.—(λ) With abl. of means or cause: de quibus (discordiis) ipsis his prodigiis a dis immortalibus admonemur,: proximi diei casu admoniti omnia ad defensionem paraverunt,: divinā admonitus plagā,.—
Esp.
To recall a thing to memory, to bring to remembrance (without any accessory notion of admonition); with acc. or gen.: cum memor anteactos semper dolor admonet annos, Müll. (some read here admovet): admonuit dominae deseruitque Venus,: nomen, quod possit equorum Admonuisse,.—
Of a creditor, to remind a debtor of his debt, to ask payment, to dun: cum tibi cotidie potestas hominis fuisset admonendi, verbum nullum facis,; so —
In the poets and in later Lat., to urge or incite to action (cf. admonitor): telo admonuit bijugos,; so : liberos verberibus,;

la:noun:admiratio.html:
admīrātĭo, ōnis, f.
admiror
.
An admiring, admiration.—Absol.: tua divina virtus admirationis plus habet quam gloriae,: qui (plausus) non numquam ipsa admiratione compressus est,: perspicua admiratione declaratur,; .— More freq. with gen. of object: copiose sapienterque dicentis,: si quid fuit in isto studio admirationis,: admiratione afficiuntur ii,: admiratio nonnulla in bestiis aquatilibus,: cuivis inicere admirationem sui,: hominis admiratio,: admiratio viri,; so ; : in magna admiratione esse,to be greatly admired,.—In plur.: haec sunt, quae admirationes in bonis oratoribus efficiunt,; so ; .—
Wonder, surprise, astonishment (cf.: admiror, admirabilis): hoc mihi maximam admirationem movet,; so, habere,: divitiarum,; ; : admiratio ancipitis sententiae,: non sine admiratione,; so ; : ut admirationem faciam populo,: miratus sum illam admiratione magna,.—Also with quod: (Decium) admiratio incessit, quod nec pugnam inirent, etc.,.

senses: To be surprised at; to be astonished
la:verb:admiror.html:
ad-mīror, ātus, 1, v. dep.,
to wonder at, to be astonished at, to regard with admiration, to admire, to be in a state of mind in which something pleases us by its extraordinary greatness, its sublimity, or perfection; while mirari signifies to be surprised at, to have the feeling of the new, singular, unusual.
In gen.: quorum ego copiam non modo non contemno, sed etiam vehementer admiror,: ingenium tuum, Crasse, vehementer admirans,fin.: res gestas,: quem et admiror et diligo,; so : magnitudinem animi,; ; : illum, (cf. mirari in , and the Gr. θαυμάζειν, Eurip. Med. 1144).—
Esp.
To gaze at passionately, to strive after a thing from admiration of it, to desire to obtain it: nihil hominem nisi quod honestum decorumque sit, aut admirari aut optare aut expetere oportere,: nil admirari prope res est una, Numici, Solaque quae possit facere et servare beatum, not to be brought by any thing into an impassioned state of mind, or into a state of desire or longing (as in the Gr. μὴ θαυμάζειν; acc. to Pythagoras the limit of all philos. effort),.—
More freq., to fall into a state of wonder or astonishment at a thing, to wonder at, be astonished at.—Constr. with acc., acc. with inf., de, super aliquam rem, with a relat. clause, quod, cur, etc.: quid admirati estis?why are you so surprised?: admiratus sum brevitatem epistulae,: hoc maxime admiratus sum, mentionem te hereditatum ausum esse facere,; so ; : de diplomate admiraris, quasi, etc.,: de Dionysio sum admiratus, qui, etc.,; so : super quae admiratus pater,; : cave quidquam admiratus sis, quā causā id fiat,: admirantium, unde hoc studium exstitisset,: admiratur quidnam Vettius dicturus sit,: admiror, quo pacto, etc.,: admiratus sum, quod, etc.,: ne quis sit admiratus, cur, etc.,. !*? Pass.: Propter venustatem vestimentorum admirari, to be admired, Canutius ap. P.—Part. fut. pass.: admīrandus, a, um, to be admired; admirable, wonderful: suspicienda et admiranda,: quo magis pravitas eorum admiranda est,. —Hence also adj., = admirabilis: patiens admirandum in modum,: exposuit quae in Italia viderentur admiranda, id. Cat. fin.: admiranda spectacula,: vir subtilis et in plurimis admirandus,.—Comp. and adv. not used.—Sup. is found in : admirandissimi juvenes; cf. Barth, Adv. 35, 9.

senses: to take charge of, direct, manage, administer, do, accomplish; govern
la:verb:administro.html:
ad-mĭnistro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Lit., to be near as an aid, to attend upon, to assist, to serve (ministrum esse ad aliquam rem): conductam esse eam, quae hic administraret ad rem divinam tibi,: omnia per sacerdotes administrabuntur,: David in sua generatione cum administrasset,: mel ad principia convivii et in secundam mensam administratur,is served up,.—Hence, with esp. ref. to the object,
Fig., to take charge of, to manage, guide, administer, execute, accomplish, do, perform, etc. (the most usual signif. of this word; very freq. in Cic. and the histt.): a nobis omnia populi R. semper et belli adjumenta et pacis ornamenta administrata sunt,; so, provinciam,to govern,: leges et judicia,: rem publicam,; so ; cf. Drak. : bellum,; (a military t. t.); cf. with exercitus,; Herz. ad , and Cortius ad ; ; ; ; : rem familiarem,: negotium alicujus,: neque ab uno omnia imperia administrari poterant,be issued, given,: classem,: navem,to guide, steer,: legionarii, qui dextram partem operis administrabant,i. e. who conducted the siege on the right side,: illustriores legationes,: oppida et fines alicujus,; cf. also ; ; ; ; so absol. (the acc. must be supplied from that which precedes): neque administrandi (sc. navigium) neque repellendi facultas dabatur,: milites neque pro opere consistere neque inter vineas sine periculo administrare poterant,nor ... pursue their work without peril,: si celeriter administraverint (sc. hoc opus), Rod. (others translate administrare in this place, to put the hand to, to render service, to do one's duty, etc.).—Unus.: virtutem, innocentiam, diligentiam alicujus, to employ, Cato ap. .

la:noun:admonitio.html:
admŏnĭtĭo, ōnis, f.
admoneo
.
A reminding, recalling to mind, suggestion: illud ne indignuin quidem admonitione, ingens in epilogis verti discrimen,: tanta vis admonitionis inest in locis, ut, etc.,: qua admonitione succurrit quod Varro tradit, etc.,: unius admonitione verbi in memoriam reponuntur,: unius admonitione verbi,.—Hence, transf.: admonitio morbi, or doloris, the returning sensations of a former sickness: si qua admonitio doloris supersit,: admonitionem morbi sentire,.—
A friendly, mild admonition (cf. : admonitio, quasi lenior objurgatio; v. admoneo, 1.): admonitio et praeceptum,; so : si aliter sentirem certe admonitio tua me reprimere aut si dubitarem, hortatio impellere posset, Planc. ap. .—
Correction, chastise ment: plures admonitione notavit,: admonitio fustium,.

la:adv:admodum.html:
ad-mŏdum, adv.
modus
, prop.,
to the measure or limit (scarcely found in the poets, except the comic poets); as, postea ubi occipiet fervere, paulisper demittito, usque admodum dum quinquies quinque numeres,quite to the limit till you count, until you count, (like fere and omnino, freq. put after its word).— Hence,
To a (great) measure, in a high degree, much, very.—With adj., P. adj., vbs., and adv.
With adj.: admodum causam gravem, Müll.: admodum antiqui,: admodum amplum et excelsum,: utrique nostrum gratum admodum feceris,; so : nec admodum in virum honorificum,: in quo multum admodum fortunae datur,: neque admodum sunt multi,: admodum magnis itineribus,: admodum pauci,; ; ; : pauci admodum,: iter angustum admodum,: admodum nimia ubertas,very excessive,: admodum dives,: brevis admodum,.—And strengthened by quam, q. v. (only before and after the class. per.): hic admodum quam saevus est,very cruel indeed,: voce admodum quam suavi, (on this use of quam, cf. Rudd. II. p. 307, n. 15).—
With part. adj.: admodum iratum senem,: iratum admodum,: natio admodum dedita religionibus,: prorae admodum erectae,: admodum mitigati,: munitus admodum,: admodum fuit militum virtus laudanda,.—Esp. is it joined (like κομιδῇ in Dem.) with words denoting age; as, puer, adulescens, juvenis, senex, to enhance the idea (for which in some cases the dim. or the prefix per- is used; as, puellus, adulescentulus, peradulescentulus): Catulus admodum tum adulescens,; ; : puer admodum,; ; : admodum infans,: juvenis admodum,: fratres admodum juvenes,: admodum senex,: admodum parvulus,: non admodum grandem natu,.— Also with dim.: neque admodum adulescentulus est, Naev. ap. Sergium ad Don. Keil, Gr. Lat. IV. p. 559 (R): hic admodum adulescentulus est,; so (cf. peradulescentulus, ), and .—
With verbs (in earlier Latin, mostly with delectare, diligere, placere): haec anus admodum frigultit, Enn. ap. : irridere ne videare et gestire admodum,: neque admodum a pueris abscessit,: me superiores litterae tuae admodum delectaverunt,; : ejus familiarissimos, qui me admodum diligunt,: stomacho admodum prodest,: bucinum pelagio admodum adligatur,: (familia) ipsa admodum floruit,: Marius auctis admodum copiis ... vicit, Halm.—
With adv.: haec inter nos nuper notitia admodum est,: si quando demersimus, aut nihil superum aut obscure admodum cernimus, ap. : acipenser, qui admodum raro capitur, id. de Fato ap. : raro admodum admonitu amicorum ... uti solebat,: ubi satis admodum suorum animos est expertus, Weissenb. (Hertz cancels satis): quae maxime admodum oratori accommodata est, Auct. ad (Oudendorp regarded this as a mere pleonasm, and Hand seems to agree with him; Klotz and B. and K. adopt after Goerenz the reading maxime ad modum oratoris, but Hand condemned this form).—
To a (full) measure, fully, completely, wholly, quite, absolutely.
Of number (not used in this way by Cic., Tac., or Suet.): noctu turres admodum CXX. excitantur, full 120, : sex milia hostium caesa; quinque admodum Romanorum,. 14; 42, 65, 3; 44, 43, 8: mille admodum hostium utràque pugnā occidit,: in laevo cornu Bactriani ibant equites, mille admodum,a round thousand,: mille admodum equites praemiserat, quorum paucitate Alexander, etc., a thousand, but not more (as the context requires), : congregati admodum quingenti sponsos hostes consectantur, trucidatisque admodum novem milibus, etc.,. !*? The meaning, circiter, fere, about, near, or nearly, which used to be assigned to this head, as by Graevius ad , Gronovius ad , is rejected by recent scholars, as Hand, Turs. I. p. 175 sq., and by Corradini, Lex. Lat. s. h. v.
Of time: legati ex Macedonia exacto admodum mense Februario redierunt,when February was fully ended,: Alexandri filius, rex Syriae, decem annos admodum habens,just ten years,: post menses admodum septem occiditur,.—
With negatives, just, at all, absolutely: equestris pugna nulla admodum fuit,no engagement with the cavalry at all,: armorum magnam vim transtulit, nullam pecuniam admodum,: horunc illa nibilum quidquam facere poterit admodum,: Curio litterarum admodum nihil sciebat,: oratorem plane quidem perfectum et cui nihil admodum desit, Demosthenem facile dixeris,: alter non multum, alter nihil admodum scripti reliquit (by the latter is meant Antonius, who indeed, acc. to , left a treatise de ratione dicendi, but no written oration at all, by which his eloquence could be judged), ; ; ; ειρωνεια a tropo genere ipso nihil admodum distat, ; quia nihil admodum super vite aut arbore colenda sciret,. —
In emphatic affirmative or corroborative answers, = maxime (Gr. πάνυ γε), exactly, just so, quite so, certainly, yes (freq. in Plaut., only twice in Ter.); cf. the remark of Cic.: scis solere, frater, in hujusmodi sermone, ut transiri alio possit, dici Admodum aut Prorsus ita est, Leg. 3, 11, 26: nempe tu hanc dicis, quam esse aiebas dudum popularem meam. Tr. Admodum, Certainly, : num quidnam ad filium haec aegritudo attinet? Ni. Admodum, It does, ; ; ; ; ; : Advenis modo? Pa. Admodum, Yes, ; .!*? Admodum with an adj. may have the same force as in II., in: quandam formam ingenii, sed admodum impolitam et plane rudem,absolutely without polish and altogether rude,, compared with: (oratorem) plane perfectum et cui nihil admodum desit,, where the same adverbs occur.

senses: surprising, astonishing, amazing, rare, strange, producing wonder
la:adj:admirabilis.html:
admīrābĭlis, e, adj.
admiror
.
Worthy of admiration, admirable, wonderful: admirabilis in dicendo vir,: O clementiam admirabilem,: gravitatem atque constantiam,: scientia,.— Ironically: o admirabilem impudentiam, audaciam, temeritatem,; so, o admirabilior oratio,: magnitudo pop. R. admirabilior adversis rebus quam secundis,: admirabilem licentiam,: quam admirabile est nomen,: de tenebris vos vocavit in admirabile lumen suum, Pet. 2, 9.—
That produces wonder, wonderful, astonishing, strange, rare, paradoxical: haec παράδοξα ili, nos admirabilia dicamus, ; cf. id. Par. praef. and Par. 4: admirabile genus (causae), a quo alienatus est animus eorum qui audituri sunt,: concursus,: gloria,.—Comp.: non esse admirabilius Romanos Graeciā pelli quam Hannibalem Italiā pulsum esse,; also .—Sup. not used.—Adv.: admīrābĭlĭter (only in the posit.).
Admirably, ; ; .—
Paradoxically, strangely, παραδόξως,

la:noun:administratio.gloss: administration, management, government (of a city, body)
senses: administration, management, government (of a city, body)
la:noun:administratio.html:
admĭnistrātĭo, ōnis, f.
administro
.
Lit., a ministration, aid, assistance: quae nec haberemus, nisi manus et ars accessissent, nec his sine hominum administratione uteremur,: aquae,the right distribution of,.— Hence,
Fig., the direction, management, or administration of a thing, i. q. curatio, procuratio: utrum (di) omni curatione et administratione rerum vacent,: rerum magnarum agitatio atque administratio,: mundi,; so ; : portūs,the use of,; ; ; ; so absol.: Ideo habentes administrationem,ministry,.

la:verb:administrandus.gloss: which is to be attended or served
senses: which is to be attended or served

la:verb:admittendus.gloss: which is to be let in; which is to be admitted
senses: which is to be let in; which is to be admitted

la:verb:admoveo.gloss: to move, bring, conduct, lead or carry someone or something to or toward; apply to
senses: to move, bring, conduct, lead or carry someone or something to or toward; apply to
to move or bring someone or something near to another; reconcile
to move or bring up or forward, call upon
to apply, attend or direct to or toward
to put one's hand to an undertaking
to lay violent hands upon; attack, assault
la:verb:admoveo.html:
ad-mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2, v. a. (admōram, admōrim, etc., sync. for admoveram, admoverim, etc., ; ),
to move a person or thing; to bring, conduct, lead, carry, etc., to or toward a place (syn.: adduco, adicio, adhibeo, appello).
Lit.
In gen., constr. with ad or with dat. (in the histt., of an army, implements for besieging, etc.; class. at all periods): dum ne exercitum propius urbem Romam CC milia admoveret, : copias in locum,: signa Achradinae,ext.; so : castra,.—Hence, also, sometimes absol., to draw near, to approach, to bring near: jam admovebat rex,: jam opera admoventi deditio est facta,: scalas moenibus,. —Trop.: quot admovi illi fabricas! quot fallacias! (where formerly admoenivi was erroneously read): tamquam aliquā machinā admotā, capere Asinii adulescentiam,; so also: ignes ardentesque laminae ceterique cruciatus admovebantur (sc. civi Romano),: dolorum faces,: cumque quasi faces ei doloris admoverentur,: fasciculum ad nares,fin.: pecus flagrantibus aris,: admotae hostiae (sc. aris),; so ; : Hannibalem admotum, i. e. adductum altaribus, led or conducted to, : labra poculis,: ignes templis,: exercitum Ariminum,: vultum ad auditores,: animam admotis fugientem sustinet herbis,: (opes) Stygiis admoverat umbris,: manus operi,to apply,: capiti diadema,: digitum scripturae,: oscula,to give a kiss,: aliquem ad munera publica,to promote, advance,: infantes papillae,to put to,: gressum,to approach nearer, (cf.: addere gressum).—
Esp.
To bring one thing near to another, and in the pass.poet. of places, to lie or be situated near: nocturna ad lumina linum nuper ubi extinctum admoveas,: quae nisi admoto igne ignem concipere possit,: culina ut sit admota, i. e. near or close by, : genus admotum Superis,nearly related,: admota Nilo Africa,.—Hence, aliquem alicui, to bring one near another, i. e. to make friends, to reconcile: mors Agrippae admovit propius Neronem Caesari,.—
With the access. idea of regard to an object to be attained, to move, bring, or apply a thing to; e. g. admovere aures (or aurem), to lend an ear to: manus (or manum) operi, to put one's hand to a work, etc.: accessi, adstiti, animam (my breath) compressi, aurem admovi, : admovere aures et subauscultando excipere voces, (cf.: aures adhibere,: praebere aures,; and: tenere aures,); and aures, poet. for auditores: cum tibi sol tepidus plures admoverit aures,: admovent manus vectigalibus populi Rom.,; ; : in marmoribus, quibus Nicias manum admovisset,which he had put his hand to,; : ruderibus purgandis manus primus admovit,. But sometimes manus admovere signif., to lay violent hands on, to attack or assault: numquam deos ipsos admovere nocentibus manus, al.—
Fig., of mental objects, to put, apply, or direct to any thing: quid praedicem ... quot stimulos admoverit homini,put the goad to,: mulier saevissima est, Cum stimulos odio pudor admovet,: num admoveri possit oratio ad sensus animorum inflammandos,: animis judicum admovere orationem, tamquam fidibus manum,: sed alia quaedam sit ad eum admovenda curatio (just before: adhibenda oratio; cf. adhibeo),: mentem ad voces alicujus, to direct to, attend to, Auct. Harusp. Resp. 10: serus enim Graecis admovit acumina chartis, not until late did (the Roman) apply his wits to Greek literature, : terrorem,to strike with terror,; : spes est admota,: spes cupiditati admota occaecavit animum,; : desiderium patriae, to instil or infuse,

la:verb:admisceo.gloss: to mix or mingle with, in or together, admix, combine, add to, blend
senses: to mix or mingle with, in or together, admix, combine, add to, blend
to involve or entangle in something
to interfere or meddle with, get involved
la:verb:admisceo.html:
ad-miscĕo, scui, xtum (better than -stum), 2, v. a.,
to add to by mingling, to mix with, mingle with, to admix (in admiscere there is a ref. to a principal constituent, to which something is added; in immiscere, to the intimate union of the ingredients; in permiscere, to the removal of their distinct characteristics).
Lit., constr. with the abl. of that with which any thing is mingled: aër multo calore admixtus, (cf. on the contr. ib. § 26: aquae admixtum calorem; and soon after: admixtum calorem): genus radicis admixtum lacte,.— With in with acc.: admixtis in heminam seminis resinae coclearibus duobus,.—With cum: admiscent torrefacta sesama cum aniso,.—
Transf.
Of things, to mingle in, to mix with, to add to, etc.: nec tamen admiscent in eorum corpus inane,: deus bonis omnibus mundum implevit; mali nihil admiscuit,: se admiscere atque implicare hominum vitiis, id. Fragm. ap. : sed hoc cum iis rationibus admisceri nolo,be mixed up,: admiscere huic generi orationis illud alterum,: versus admiscere orationi,: admiscenda venus est timori,: non admixtus fidei,; .—
Of persons.
To mix up with, to add or join to: his Antonianos milites admiscuerat,. 4: expeditos antesignanos admiscuit,fin.: ad id consilium admisceor,: admiscerenturne plebeii,i. e. whether the plebeians should be admitted to the number of the decemvirs,: admixti funditoribus sagittarii,; .—
To involve or entangle in a thing: se, to interfere or meddle with: ita tu istaec tua misceto, ne me admisceas,: ne te admisce: nemo accusat, Syre, te,: ad id consilium admiscear?: Trebatium vero meum, quod isto admisceas nihil est,implicate, involve in,.—Hence, admixtus, a, um, P. a., that is mingled with something, mixed, not simple: simplex animi natura est, nec habet in se quidquam admixtum,: nihil est animis admixtum, nihil concretum, nihil copulatum, nihil coagmentatum, nihil duplex,.—Comp., sup., and adv. not used.

la:verb:adminiculo.html:
admĭnĭcŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
adminiculum
(orig. belonging to agriculture and botany),
to prop up, to support.
Lit.: vites adminiculatae sudibus,; so Col.: vitem adminiculato arborique jungito, de Arb. 16 (Cic. has for this adminiculor, q. v.).—
Trop., = adjuvo (only ante- and post-class.): adminiculavi voluntatem tuam scribendo, Varr. ap. : tribunicio auxilio adminiculati, id. ap. P.: id ipsum, quod dicimus, ex illis quoque Homericis versibus adminiculari potest, i. e. confirmari, ; so : Di vitam hominum adminiculantes,.—Hence Müll., calls adverbs partes adminiculandi (orationem), auxiliaries of discourse.—Hence, admĭnĭcŭlātus, a, um, P. a., supported; hence, well furnished or provided: memoria adminiculatior, Gell. praef. 1. 1.

ad-manus
, prop.,

Lit.
Orig. in the language of vine-dressers, the stake or pole to which the vine clings, and by which it is supported: vites claviculis adminicula, tamquam manibus apprehendunt, atque ita se erigunt, ut animantes,: adminiculorum ordines, capitum jugatio,; so ; cf. Drak. .— Hence,
In gen., of any prop, stay, or support, assistance: adminicula hominum, i. e. oxen, implements of agriculture, etc., ; : motam (Junonem) sede sua parvi molimenti adminiculis,: adminicula gubernandi addidit Tiphys,means of steering, the rudder,; cf. . —
Trop., support, aid, auxiliary, assistant (class.): ad legionem cum itant, adminiculum eis danunt aliquem cognatum,an assistant,: hanc igitur partem relictam explebimus, nullis adminiculis, sed, ut dicitur, Marte nostro,: natura solitarium nihil amat, semperque ad aliquod tamquam adminiculum adnititur,: quo primo adminiculo erecta erat (urbs), eodem innisa M. Furio principe stetit,: id senectuti suae adminiculum fore,: egere adminiculis, ut in commune consulat,; so, in militia aut via fessus adminiculum oro,: nullius externi indigens adminiculi,; ; : Quibus debetis esse adminiculo,.
